Fundamental — what it's worth: A weighted what-if off the published fair value — not a re-run DCF, and it never touches the Monte Carlo section below. The sizes come from the study’s own sensitivity grids, each of which re-runs the whole three-line unit build. Note which lever dominates: the terminal risk-free rate, not the operations — because three quarters of the operating value sits in the terminal block, and that one input is the only major assumption in the study still resting on a convention rather than a source. The top lever is the one thing the published number does not contain at all.
Technical & price structure: In plain terms: the company has just finished a USD 100 million biologicals plant. From FY2026 its AED 4,901 million construction balance — larger than the entire depreciated property base before it — starts depreciating, and this study charges every pound of that while crediting the plant with NO revenue, because the company has published none. That is why the fundamental readings cluster at AED 58–73 against a price of AED 130.05. Read the other way: the market is paying AED 72.01 a share, 55% of the price, for that plant — roughly 2.1 times what it cost to build — which needs about USD 120 million a year of biosimilar revenue by FY2030 to justify. That is the bet, and it is a number the company will eventually disclose.
Monte Carlo — where could the price go?: Our fundamental range tops out at AED 0.95 even in the bull case — so unlike most names we cover, the whole simulated price cone sits ABOVE the fair-value range, not around it. Read that gap for what it is: the simulation prices where the tape can travel over three months, the study prices what the business is worth. A sustained move above AED 0.95 on the fundamentals — collection landing, margins recovering, rates falling — is the point where we’d rebuild the study.

One Monte Carlo model, 50,000 paths, driven by the outside forces relevant to a hard-currency industrial exporter listed in a soft-currency market: the LME copper price, the AED/USD path, the CBE policy corridor and the pace of easing, the United Arab Emiratesian inflation, Gulf and North African grid and infrastructure spending, the order book and its conversion rate, interconnector and data-centre demand for cable and transformers, energy and freight costs, convertibility and repatriation risk on the foreign earnings, and the free float — 11.6% of the shares, with 68% held by the family and 20% by Electra, which is what makes the tape thin.
